text: From that time on no one tried to remove the veil. <break time="0.8s" /> And Mister Hooper became a man apart. <break time="0.8s" /> For people avoided him. <break time="0.8s" /> And children fled at his approach. <break time="0.8s" /> Hating the veil himself. <break time="0.8s" /> He never passed a mirror. <break time="0.8s" /> Nor stooped to drink at a still fountain. <break time="0.8s" /> Lest he should be frightened. <break time="0.8s" /> By his own reflection. <break time="0.8s" /> Gossips whispered. <break time="0.8s" /> That some great crime lay hidden. <break time="0.8s" /> Behind the black crape. <break time="0.8s" /> And a cloud of sin or sorrow. <break time="0.8s" /> Seemed to wrap the poor minister. <break time="0.8s" /> Wherever he went. <break time="0.8s" /> Yet the veil had one desirable effect. <break time="0.8s" /> For it made him a very efficient clergyman. <break time="0.8s" /> With awful power over souls. <break time="0.8s" /> That were in agony for sin. <break time="0.8s" /> Dying sinners called for Mister Hooper. <break time="0.8s" /> And would not breathe their last. <break time="0.8s" /> Until he appeared. <break time="0.8s" /> Though they always shuddered. <break time="0.8s" /> When the veiled face bent over them. <break time="0.8s" /> Once, under Governor Belcher. <break time="0.8s" /> He preached the election sermon. <break time="0.8s" /> And his words made so deep an impression. <break time="0.8s" /> That the laws of that year. <break time="0.8s" /> Were full of gloom and piety. <break time="0.8s" /> In this manner Mister Hooper spent a long life. <break time="0.8s" /> Kind and loving though unloved. <break time="0.8s" /> Shunned in times of joy. <break time="0.8s" /> But always summoned. <break time="0.8s" /> In times of mortal anguish. <break time="0.8s" /> As years wore on shedding their snows above his black veil. <break time="0.8s" /> He won a name. <break time="0.8s" /> Throughout the New England churches. <break time="0.8s" /> And people called him Father Hooper.
